text: Activity performed under privileged access is captured in logs and periodically reviewed by Information Security.
User access to systems is provisioned only on the basis of approved role-based requests.
Each quarter, managers review and recertify the access held by users on their teams.
Each business day, Payment Operations compares ACH originator exposure against approved limits.
The BSA Officer receives a weekly report on the aging of open AML alerts.
Payment Operations screens each outgoing payment against applicable sanctions lists in real time and releases it only after screening is complete.
On an annual basis, Treasury performs a test to confirm the bank can access its contingent funding lines.
Customer complaints are captured in a central log and monitored by the Complaints Manager until each one is resolved and closed.
Each quarter, Compliance reviews customer complaint trends to identify recurring issues and emerging risks.
On an annual basis, ALCO reviews and approves the key assumptions used in ALM modeling.
Before any contract is executed, third-party risk management performs due diligence on the prospective vendor.
Payment Operations reconciles the payment suspense accounts each business day so that unresolved items get identified and cleared on time.
Each manual posting is reviewed and approved by a second person, independent of the preparer, before it takes effect.
Before any loan is approved, underwriters review and confirm the borrower's income documentation against the verification checklist.
Payment Operations confirms each wire exceeding the established threshold through a callback to the customer before the wire is released.

For each request for access to an in-scope application, the user's manager and the application owner review and approve it through Okrin Identity Gateway before any access is granted. The gateway routes every submitted request to both approvers and holds provisioning until both approvals are recorded. Requests for access that falls outside the role catalogue also need sign-off from Information Security before they can proceed. When a user changes role, the gateway removes their existing access automatically, and the request, approval and removal history it retains for each user serves as evidence of the control's operation.

Each quarter, Information Security launches a recertification campaign in Okrin Identity Gateway that covers every entitlement on the critical applications in scope. The responsible manager reviews each assigned entitlement and either certifies that access is still needed or marks it for revocation, and Information Security removes any revoked access within five business days of the manager's decision. At campaign close, Information Security identifies campaigns with uncertified items and reports them to the Technology Risk Committee. Retained evidence includes the campaign completion export from Okrin Identity Gateway with each reviewer's decision and timestamp, the revocation completion dates measured against the five-day standard, and the committee materials showing the incomplete-campaign report.

Corvessa Core Banking applies a system hold that prevents activation of any new legal entity account until every beneficial ownership certification field has been populated and marked as verified by the onboarding team. This preventive control operates automatically at the point of account opening, so an account cannot be released to transact while any required certification field remains blank or unverified. Separately, customer risk ratings are recalculated in a nightly batch using current ownership and account activity data. Evidence retained includes the system configuration settings for the activation hold, the record of onboarding verification for each certified account, and the nightly batch logs for the risk rating recalculation.

Each year, BSA Compliance performs above- and below-the-line testing on every scenario configured in Merrow AML Monitor, sampling alerted and non-alerted activity around current thresholds to judge whether each threshold is still set appropriately. As part of the same annual review, the team confirms that every product and channel offered by the bank maps to at least one active scenario and updates the coverage mapping to reflect any gaps or changes. Any resulting threshold adjustment requires BSA Officer approval and independent validation by Model Risk before it is implemented in production. Evidence retained includes the testing workpapers and sample results, the signed product and channel coverage map, the BSA Officer's documented approval, and the Model Risk validation memo for each threshold change.

Before any wire is released, Brisance Wire Manager automatically screens each incoming and outgoing transfer against the sanctions list, and list updates load into the system on the same day they are published. Any potential match holds the payment in queue until Compliance reviews it, records the disposition, and either releases or blocks the wire. Evidence retained for testing includes the system log of list update load dates and, for each potential match, the documented Compliance review showing the reviewer, the rationale and the final release or block decision.

Once a year, Treasury reviews the deposit runoff assumptions used in liquidity stress testing against recent stress events and the bank's current concentration of uninsured deposits. For each runoff rate, Treasury writes a rationale explaining why the rate was kept or changed in light of that comparison. Market Risk independently challenges the assumptions and rationale before the package goes to ALCO for approval. Evidence retained includes the comparison workpaper, the rate-by-rate rationale, Market Risk's written challenge and Treasury's responses, and the ALCO minutes recording approval.

Once each year, Treasury executes a small-dollar test draw against every contingent funding source, including the FHLB advance line and the Federal Reserve discount window, to confirm the facilities work in practice. During each draw, Treasury reconciles its record of pledged collateral values to the values confirmed by the lender and logs the elapsed time from request to receipt of funds. Treasury then presents the test results to ALCO, including any step that failed, with a named owner and target completion date for each remediation item. Evidence retained includes draw confirmations, lender collateral statements, the time-to-funds log and the ALCO minutes and presentation.

Branch and contact center staff enter every customer complaint into Tessaly Case Manager no later than one business day after receipt, and this includes complaints customers raise verbally at a branch. The Complaints Manager is alerted whenever a case stays unresolved for more than 15 days and works it to closure. Each month the Complaints Manager prepares an aging report from Tessaly Case Manager covering these escalated items and presents it to the Compliance Committee. Evidence retained consists of the case records with intake timestamps, the escalation history, and the monthly report together with Compliance Committee minutes.

Each quarter, Compliance extracts complaint data from Tessaly Case Manager and analyzes volumes and trends by product, channel and theme to find emerging or recurring issues. When a theme exceeds the established threshold, Compliance assigns a root cause owner who must investigate the underlying cause and propose corrective actions. Compliance then tracks each corrective action to closure, following up on open items in later quarterly cycles until they are resolved. Evidence retained includes the quarterly analysis workpaper with the Tessaly Case Manager extract, documented owner assignments for above-threshold themes, and the corrective action tracking log showing status and closure dates.

Each quarter, Treasury compares the deposit beta and prepayment speed assumptions in Pellmark ALM against actual observed results, and any variance that exceeds the established tolerance is reported to ALCO with an explanation of its cause and any proposed assumption change. Evidence retained for this step includes the quarterly back-testing workpaper and the ALCO meeting package and minutes that reflect the variance discussion. On an annual basis, ALCO reviews and approves the full assumption set, with approval documented in the ALCO minutes. Model Risk performs an independent validation of the model every two years, and the resulting validation report and any findings are retained as evidence.

Before any new product or material product change goes live, the product owner presents the New Product Committee with a completed risk assessment that carries sign-off from Compliance, Operational Risk and Information Security. The committee reviews the package at its scheduled meeting, and no launch may proceed until the committee has recorded its approval in the meeting minutes. Within six months after go-live, a post-implementation review is performed and its results are reported back to the committee. Retained evidence consists of the signed risk assessment, the committee minutes documenting approval and the launch date, and the completed post-implementation review, all kept in the committee's product file.

Each business day, Payment Operations staff reconcile the balance of every payment suspense account to Velistra General Ledger and identify the open items that make up any difference. Open items aged beyond 15 days are escalated to the operations manager for follow-up, and items aged beyond 30 days are escalated to the Controller. No suspense item may be written off without Controller approval. The completed daily reconciliation, the aged-item listing with escalation notes, and the approved write-off requests are retained as evidence of performance and review.

Before any loan can move to booking, Halbrook Loan Origination automatically checks the assigned approver's delegated lending authority against the approval matrix and blocks booking when the requested amount or terms fall outside that authority. Any override of this check is routed to Credit Administration. Each week, Credit Administration reviews the system override log, confirms that every override carries a documented approval, and escalates any item lacking one to the Chief Credit Officer for resolution. Retained evidence includes the system-generated override log, the reviewer's sign-off on each weekly review, and the escalation correspondence sent to the Chief Credit Officer along with its disposition.

Before each loan closes, valuation unit staff order the third-party appraisal from the approved appraiser panel and review the completed report against a standard review checklist. The checklist confirms that comparable sales are relevant and adequately adjusted, that the appraiser is independent of the borrower and the loan production function, and that the concluded value is supported. Any valuation dated more than 120 days before the closing date is re-ordered rather than relied upon. The signed and dated checklist, the appraisal report and any re-order request are kept in the loan file as evidence of performance.

Before any outgoing wire exceeding $25,000, or any wire to a beneficiary not previously paid, is released, operations staff place an independent callback to the customer using the telephone number on file in Corvessa Core Banking rather than any number supplied with the wire request. The operator logs the callback in Brisance Wire Manager, noting the date and time, the number dialed, the individual reached and confirmation of the beneficiary and amount details. Release is blocked in Brisance Wire Manager until a second operator reviews and approves the callback record, so the performer and approver are always different people. The callback log entry and the second operator's approval are retained in Brisance Wire Manager as evidence of control performance for each qualifying wire.

Internal Audit found that above- and below-the-line testing of transaction monitoring scenarios is not operating as designed. Remote deposit capture activity has not been mapped to any monitoring scenario, so those transactions fall outside automated surveillance. In addition, the required below-the-line testing was not performed for 5 of the 18 scenarios in the current scenario inventory, leaving thresholds for those scenarios unvalidated.

Internal Audit found that Treasury did not execute a test draw on the discount window at any point during 2024, leaving the bank's ability to access contingent funding through that channel unvalidated. In addition, the collateral schedules supporting FHLB and discount window borrowing capacity had last been updated nine months before the review, so reported availability could not be relied upon for liquidity planning.

During second-line testing of third-party onboarding, we found that four vendors classified as critical had been approved and onboarded before their due diligence was complete, with open items still outstanding at contract execution. For one of the four, no SOC 2 report had been obtained or reviewed before onboarding, and nothing in the file showed that a compensating assessment of the vendor's control environment had been performed.

Examiners determined that Treasury did not execute a test draw on the Federal Reserve discount window at any point during 2024 as part of the annual contingency funding test. Collateral schedules supporting the contingency funding plan were also found to be nine months out of date at the time of review, which limits the bank's ability to rely on pledged collateral values under stress.

During a review of the vendor inventory, management found that four vendors rated as critical had been onboarded and placed into service before their due diligence reviews were closed. For one of these four, no SOC 2 report had been obtained at the time of onboarding, so the bank had no independent assurance over that vendor's control environment.

During second line testing of third-party onboarding, four vendors rated critical were found to have been onboarded and placed under contract while their due diligence remained open. For one of these vendors, no SOC 2 report had been obtained at the time of review, so the control environment of a critical service provider was not assessed before the relationship began.

Our review of complaint handling found that complaints received at branches were not entered into the tracking process promptly, with an average lag of nine days between receipt and logging. In addition, 31 complaints remained open beyond 15 days with no evidence of escalation. These conditions limit management's ability to monitor complaint resolution timeliness and to identify potential UDAAP concerns.

Internal Audit found that complaints received at branches were entered into the central complaint log an average of nine days after receipt, which leaves little of the 15-day resolution window for tracking and follow-up. Within the review population, 31 complaints exceeded 15 days with no escalation to the Complaints Manager, so the log's resolution tracking is not functioning as intended.

Internal Audit found that the hold meant to keep legal entity accounts inactive until beneficial ownership certification is complete is not working as designed. Seven legal entity accounts were activated by manual override of the hold, and none had BSA approval for the override. Because these accounts became available for use without the required certification sign-off, the control's purpose was defeated in each case.

Internal Audit found that remote deposit capture transactions were not mapped to any transaction monitoring scenario, so activity through that channel was not subject to automated surveillance. Above- and below-the-line threshold testing was also incomplete: below-the-line testing was not performed for 5 of the 18 scenarios in production during the review period, and no documented rationale or approved exception supported the omission.

Internal Audit found that Treasury did not execute a test draw on the discount window at any point during 2024, so the bank could not show that the operational steps to access this contingent funding source work as designed. The collateral schedules supporting the draw process were nine months old at the time of review and did not reflect current pledged positions.

Internal Audit found that complaints received at branches were entered into the central complaint log an average of nine days after receipt, which leaves little of the 15-day resolution window for tracking and follow-up. In the population reviewed, 31 complaints remained open beyond 15 days with no escalation recorded, so the log's resolution tracking is not working as intended.

Internal Audit found that the control holding legal entity accounts from activation until beneficial ownership certification is complete did not operate as designed. Seven legal entity accounts were activated through a manual override of the hold, and none of the seven had BSA approval for the override.

Examination testing of user access in Velistra General Ledger identified fourteen accounts that administrators had provisioned directly, outside the established approval workflow. No documented business-line or role-based approval existed for these accounts at the time access was granted, indicating that the provisioning control can be bypassed by personnel holding administrative privileges.

During a self-assessment of privileged access, management found that three generic administrator accounts on Velistra General Ledger had never been placed in the credential vault. Privileged session logs for these accounts also received no review for four months, so administrative activity on the ledger went unmonitored during that period.

Because several legacy applications cannot support individual administrator accounts, privileged access is exercised through shared credentials that are neither logged nor subject to independent review. Changes made to production data through these accounts could therefore go undetected, impairing the integrity of records relied on for operations and reporting.

Because role definitions in critical applications are not kept current, users may accumulate access beyond what their job functions require. This could allow unauthorized transactions to be processed and sensitive data to be exposed.

Because periodic access review packs are too large for reviewers to assess meaningfully, entitlements that are no longer needed after an employee changes roles may stay active instead of being removed. This could create SoD conflicts and an opportunity for fraud through unauthorized processing or concealment of transactions.

Because originator exposure limits are set once at onboarding and never monitored afterward, originated ACH files may carry debits the account holder never authorized. When the originator cannot cover the resulting returned entries, the bank absorbs the losses.

Because investigator staffing has not kept pace with alert volumes, monitoring alerts may age beyond the required timeframes for disposition and accumulate into an investigation backlog. Any resulting late SAR filings would expose the bank to regulatory criticism and enforcement risk.

Because sanctions list updates are uploaded to the screening process manually, a missed, late or incomplete upload could leave screening running against outdated lists, so payments to sanctioned parties are not stopped. The bank would then be exposed to sanctions violations, regulatory penalties and related remediation costs.

Because operational draw-down testing of contingency funding sources tends to be deferred when markets are calm, those sources may not be accessible within the timeframes the contingency funding plan assumes, resulting in a liquidity shortfall if the bank experiences a deposit run.

Because branches have no single intake channel for customer complaints, complaints received in person or by phone at the branch level may never be logged or may not be resolved within required timeframes. This could leave customer harm unaddressed and increase the bank's UDAAP exposure.

Because complaint categories are defined too broadly to separate distinct issues, recurring complaint themes may go unanalyzed for root cause, which could allow the same customer harm to repeat and expose the bank to reputational damage.

Because deposit assumptions are not subject to an annual review and have become outdated, the ALM model may misstate earnings sensitivity to rate changes. Treasury and ALCO could then base hedging decisions on misleading rate sensitivity results, leaving the bank inappropriately hedged against interest rate movements.

Because no annual review of deposit assumptions is in place, the repricing betas that drive the earnings-at-risk measure have not been recalibrated since the shift in market rates and may no longer reflect actual depositor behavior. Interest rate sensitivity could therefore be misstated, leading to hedging decisions that rest on a distorted view of earnings exposure and leave the bank under- or over-hedged.

Because business sponsors often negotiate fintech partnership contracts before third-party risk management is engaged, a partnership may launch without due diligence on the partner's compliance program, exposing customers to harm and the bank to regulatory criticism attributed to it.

Because responsibility for reconciling payment suspense accounts is split between operations and finance, aged items may go unresearched and uncleared. This could leave balances misstated and allow losses to go undetected.

Because underwriting exceptions for missing income documentation are tracked in spreadsheets rather than within a controlled workflow, consumer loans may be approved and funded on borrower-stated income that is never subsequently verified. This could lead to elevated early payment defaults and repurchase demands from loan purchasers.

When staff skip callback verification to meet same-day cut-off times, outgoing wires may be released on payment instructions received from a compromised customer email account. Funds sent this way are often unrecoverable once credited to the beneficiary institution, which leaves the bank exposed to reimbursing the customer for the loss.

User access provisioning is part of the Access Management risk area. The audit evaluates whether access requests are properly approved before being granted, whether roles are designed so they confer only appropriate entitlements, and whether access that is no longer needed is removed promptly after an employee changes roles.

Periodic access recertification falls within the access management risk area and covers the recurring review of user entitlements by system and business owners. The audit evaluates whether reviews are complete across all in-scope users and applications, whether access flagged for removal is revoked in a timely manner, and whether SoD conflicts are identified and resolved or formally accepted.

Beneficial ownership and CDD refresh falls within the AML monitoring risk area and covers how the bank obtains and maintains beneficial ownership certifications and refreshes customer risk ratings on schedule. The audit also tests whether the monitoring scenarios applied to high-risk customers are assigned correctly and keep running after a rating changes.

AML transaction monitoring scenario tuning and coverage is a risk area in AML monitoring that covers whether detection scenarios are calibrated and cover the bank's products. The audit tests completeness of the scenario inventory, reviews above-the-line and below-the-line threshold testing that supports tuning decisions, and checks that product and transaction types map to at least one active scenario.

This AML monitoring entry covers the screening of payment transactions against sanctions lists. The audit tests whether list updates are loaded promptly, whether fuzzy-match settings are calibrated and governed appropriately, and whether screening hits are dispositioned accurately and on time with adequate supporting evidence.

Liquidity stress scenario design falls within the interest rate and liquidity risk area and covers how Treasury builds and calibrates the stress scenarios used to test funding resilience. The audit assesses whether scenario severity is adequately challenging, whether concentrations of uninsured deposits are reflected in projected outflows, and whether the deposit assumptions shared with the ALM model are consistent, documented and supported.

Under interest rate and liquidity risk, this entry covers testing of the contingency funding plan. The audit reviews plan test results and the handling of any noted exceptions, the adequacy and documentation of collateral pledged to secure contingent funding sources, and Treasury's operational readiness to access the Federal Reserve discount window on short notice.

Complaint handling, covering intake and resolution of customer complaints. The audit evaluates how complaints are captured across intake channels, whether resolution is timely, and how complaints received through regulators are tracked and answered.

Complaint trend analysis falls within the complaint handling risk area and covers how complaints are categorized, whether root cause reviews are completed for recurring issues, and the accuracy of management reporting on trends. Audit work tests a sample of logged complaints for correct coding and traces reported trend figures back to source records maintained under the Complaints Manager.

Within the interest rate and liquidity risk area, ALM model assumptions and validation covers how the bank sets, approves and documents the behavioral and market assumptions that drive its ALM modeling. The audit examines assumption governance, the back-testing of model outputs against actual results, and whether findings from model validation are tracked and resolved on time.

New product approval governance falls within the project and change governance risk area. The audit examines how the New Product Committee approves proposals and whether risk assessments are completed and documented before launch. It also tests whether post-implementation reviews are performed and their findings tracked to resolution.

Payment suspense reconciliation covers the wire and ACH suspense accounts where unmatched or unapplied payments are held until cleared. The audit tests whether each reconciliation is reviewed and signed off on time, whether aged items are tracked and escalated, and whether write-offs receive appropriate approval before posting.

This loan origination risk area covers the possibility that credit approvals proceed without enforcement of the lending authority assigned to the approver. The audit tests how the approval matrix is configured, reviews the override log for exceptions and their justification, and examines all approvals above $5 million to confirm each one was granted at the appropriate authority level.

Appraisal review and independence sits within the loan origination risk area and addresses the risk that collateral valuations are improperly influenced or inadequately reviewed. The audit evaluates how appraisals are ordered and kept separate from production staff, tests completion of the appraisal review checklist, and identifies aged valuations relied on beyond acceptable timeframes.

Wire and ACH risk area covering wire callback verification, where the audit tests whether callbacks are performed and documented before release by examining callback logs, with particular attention to high-value wires and to requests involving changed beneficiary instructions.
